item.title: 🟠 Java4Shell Vulnerability - CVE-2026-114938
item.description:
Why this matters: Infrastructure/vendor signal — compare your installed versions and support status.

CVSSv3 Score: 8.1

CVE-2026-114938Vulnerability in the Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition product of Oracle Java SE (component: Compiler). Supported versions that are affected are Oracle Java SE: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3; Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.21.0.3 and 21.0.13.0.3; Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

Revised on 2026-11-19 00:00:00

item.title: 🔴 Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

item.title: 🔴 #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Advisory at a Glance

Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
Original Publication  October 20, 2026
Executive Summary

This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. 

Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Next, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks.

item.title: 🔴 #StopRansomware: Gunra Ransomware
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Advisory at a Glance

Title #StopRansomware: Gunra Ransomware
Original Publication August 10, 2026
Executive Summary Gunra is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) used by affiliates to target government, critical infrastructure, and other organizations. The Gunra ransomware variant first appeared in 2025 and expanded to RaaS operations in 2026. The actors leverage a double-extortion model, both encrypting data and threatening to publish exfiltrated data to a dedicated leak site (DLS) if the ransom is not paid. This advisory provides technical details of the activity, as well as tailored detection and mitigation guidance to protect at-risk organizations from Gunra.
Key Actions
  • Prioritize patching known exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, including virtual private network (VPN) gateways and remote desktop protocol (RDP)-exposed infrastructure.
  • Implement and test offline, immutable backups stored in a physically separate, segmented location to ensure recoverability without ransom payment.
  • Segment networks to restrict lateral movement from an initially compromised device to other systems in the organization.
